title: Why Almost Nobody Lives in Northern Idaho
sources: People in North Idaho: own count from the 2020 census, block groups (geo/measure_population.py)
Counties: US Census Bureau; states, rivers: Natural Earth; wildernesses and national forests: US Forest Service (geo/make_regions.py)
Idaho Territory 1863 and the 1910 fire area drawn as approximate areas; routes drawn through main points (approximate)

paragraphs.text: Northern Idaho is a quarter of the state, a block of mountains and forest bigger than Vermont and New Hampshire put together.

But only about one Idahoan in five lives there, and most of them crowd into one corner. Idaho County, the biggest in the state, covers more than eight thousand square miles. Only sixteen thousand people live in it.

stat.label: Idahoans who live in the ten northern counties
stat.source: Own count: 2020 census block groups, ten northern counties (geo/measure_population.py)

shots.on_screen_text: Coeur d'Alene, where most of the north lives

stat.label: Idaho County: 16,541 people on 8,477 sq mi

paragraphs.text: So why does almost nobody live in northern Idaho?

shots.photo: File:Another Canyon View in Frank Church Wilderness.jpg

paragraphs.text: Even the map looks strange. A thin chimney of land climbs north between Washington and Montana, until at the Canadian border it is only about forty-five miles wide. And above the Salmon River, Idaho runs on a different clock: the north keeps Pacific time with Seattle, the south keeps Mountain time with Boise.

shots.on_screen_text: The Salmon River at Riggins: the time line

paragraphs.text: The answer runs through a capital that was carried off by soldiers, a fire that burned an area nearly as big as Connecticut in two days, and a valley that dug up more than a billion ounces of silver and then poisoned its own children.

shots.photo: File:BUNKER HILL LEAD SMELTER. VIEW IS FROM CENTRAL IMPOUNDMENT AREA LOOKING SOUTH. PLANT DRY IS IN CENTER FOREGROUND, SLAG FUMING PLANT IS IN RIGHT FOREGROUND, AND BAG HOUSE IS IN HAER ID,40-KELL,2-1.tif

paragraphs.text: There are six reasons, and the first one is a wall of mountains in the middle of the state.
Reason one. Northern Idaho is cut off from the rest of its own state.
Between Coeur d'Alene in the north and Boise in the south lie the Clearwater, the Salmon River and the Bitterroot mountains. It is some of the roughest country in the lower forty-eight states.

shots.photo: File:Middle Fork Salmon River Frank Church Wilderness.jpg

paragraphs.text: Much of it was never built on at all. Along the Salmon River lies the Frank Church River of No Return Wilderness, almost two and a half million acres with no roads. It is the largest single block of wilderness in the lower forty-eight. Next to it lie the Selway-Bitterroot and the Gospel Hump wildernesses, and around them millions more acres of roadless forest.

stat.label: Frank Church-River of No Return Wilderness, no roads

paragraphs.text: The river through it is called the River of No Return. In the 1800s, freight boats could ride its rapids downstream but never come back up, so at the end of each trip the boatmen broke them up and sold the wood.

shots.on_screen_text: Rapids on the Middle Fork of the Salmon
The Salmon's canyon near White Bird

paragraphs.text: On the western edge, the Snake River runs through Hells Canyon, the deepest river gorge in North America, almost eight thousand feet from rim to river.

shots.on_screen_text: Hells Canyon of the Snake River

stat.label: Hells Canyon, rim to river

paragraphs.text: So there is one road between north and south. US Highway 95 is mostly two lanes, and for about forty years it climbed over a single grade at White Bird Hill, a road of switchbacks that was the only link between the two halves of the state. The faster road over the hill opened only in 1975.

shots.on_screen_text: US 95 in the Salmon River canyon

shots.photo: File:White Bird Hill Grade, 1924 - White Bird, Idaho (50901386962).jpg

stat.label: New US 95 grade over White Bird Hill opens

paragraphs.text: East to west it was no easier. The highway along the Lochsa River over Lolo Pass, close to the route Lewis and Clark took in 1805, was finished only in 1962.

stat.label: US 12 over Lolo Pass is finished

paragraphs.text: We asked a route planner for the drive from Sandpoint in the panhandle to Boise. The road through Idaho is about four hundred and twenty miles. The road that leaves Idaho, through Washington and Oregon, is seventy miles longer, and it takes about the same time.

stat.label: Sandpoint to Boise, about 9 hours either way

paragraphs.text: That is why the north sets its clocks by Seattle. Spokane, just across the Washington line, is its big city. It shops there, flies from there and watches its television.

shots.on_screen_text: Spokane to Coeur d'Alene along I-90

shots.photo: File:City of Coeur d'Alene, from a rooftop, 2006.jpg

paragraphs.text: And when people could not get through the mountains, they could not farm them either, which brings us to the second reason: who owns the land.

chapters.title: The Land Is Not for Sale

paragraphs.text: Reason two. Most of Idaho does not belong to anyone who could live on it.

About sixty-two per cent of the state is federal land, mostly national forest. Only Nevada and Utah have a larger share. In the north the forests run almost unbroken from the Canadian border to the Salmon River. Its two national forests, the Idaho Panhandle and the Nez Perce-Clearwater, cover about seven million acres between them.

stat.label: Of Idaho is federal land (CRS)
Idaho Panhandle + Nez Perce-Clearwater national forests

paragraphs.text: Those forests were set aside for timber and water, not for towns. And in the summer of 1910 they showed what else they could do.
It had been a dry year. By August hundreds of small fires were burning across northern Idaho and western Montana. Then, on the twentieth of August, a hurricane-force wind came from the southwest.

stat.label: The wind that joined the fires

paragraphs.text: In two days the fires joined into one. They burned about three million acres, nearly as big as Connecticut. About eighty-five people died, most of them firefighters. A third of the mining town of Wallace burned.

stat.label: Burned in two days, Idaho and Montana
Most of them firefighters

paragraphs.text: That night the mayor of Wallace ordered the women and children out. Trains carried them west to Spokane and east to Missoula, and soldiers pulled men off the cars to keep them on the fire line.

shots.on_screen_text: The rail line through the burn, 1910
Burned forest above the rail line, 1910

paragraphs.text: A forest ranger called Ed Pulaski was caught in the fire with a crew of about forty-five men. He led them into an old mine tunnel, held them there at gunpoint when they panicked, and hung wet blankets across the entrance. All but five or six of them survived.

stat.label: Ed Pulaski's crew, 20 August 1910
Pulaski's crew who came out alive

paragraphs.text: The Big Burn made the young Forest Service what it became. From then on its job was to stop every fire, and by 1935 the rule was to have each one out by ten o'clock the next morning. The tool Pulaski designed after the fire, half axe and half hoe, is still carried by wildland firefighters today.

stat.label: From 1935: every fire out by 10 the next morning
The Pulaski tool, designed after the fire

paragraphs.text: The land stayed with the government, and the government kept it as forest. But to understand why the north feels it has never had a say, we have to go back to the people who drew its borders.

chapters.title: A Territory Run from Far Away

paragraphs.text: Reason three. Northern Idaho was settled first, and then it lost the state.

In 1860 a prospector called Elias Pierce found gold on the Clearwater River. Within a year thousands of miners had arrived, and a tent town grew where the Clearwater meets the Snake. They called it Lewiston.

shots.on_screen_text: Lewiston, where the Clearwater meets the Snake

paragraphs.text: The gold was on Nez Perce land. In 1863 the United States made the Nez Perce sign a new treaty that cut their reservation by about ninety per cent. Many bands never signed it, and the anger it left led to the Nez Perce War of 1877.

stat.label: Nez Perce reservation under the 1863 treaty

shots.on_screen_text: Nez Perce country on the lower Salmon

paragraphs.text: In June 1877, at White Bird Canyon, below the hill that US 95 climbs today, Nez Perce warriors routed a column of US cavalry. It was the first battle of the war. The bands that refused the treaty then fled east over the Lolo Trail, about eleven hundred and seventy miles through four states in a hundred and twenty-six days. They were caught in Montana in October, about forty miles short of Canada, and Chief Joseph surrendered.

stat.label: Battle of White Bird Canyon

shots.on_screen_text: The Lochsa, on the Nez Perce route east

stat.label: 126 days through four states

paragraphs.text: The same year, Congress created Idaho Territory, and Lewiston became its first capital. But the miners had already moved on, south to the Boise Basin, where richer gold had been found. By 1864 most of the territory's voters lived in the south.

shots.photo: File:Confluence of Clearwater and Snake rivers - Lewiston, Idaho (21116852016).jpg

stat.label: Richer gold draws the miners south
Most of the territory's voters now live in the south

paragraphs.text: In December 1864 the legislature voted to move the capital to Boise. Lewiston refused. So in 1865 the acting governor came back with soldiers from Fort Lapwai and took the territorial seal and the archives south. The territory's supreme court settled it for Boise in 1866.

stat.label: Legislature votes to move the capital to Boise
Taken from Lewiston to Boise, 1865
Court settles the capital in Boise

paragraphs.text: Then the shape. In 1864 Congress cut Montana Territory out of Idaho. Montana's border was drawn along the crest of the Bitterroot Mountains, and in the north Idaho was left with only a narrow strip of land.

shots.photo: File:Beautiful Skies over Frank Church Wilderness.jpg

paragraphs.text: The north never liked being run from Boise, nearly three hundred miles away over the mountains. In 1887 Congress actually passed a bill to give the panhandle to Washington Territory. Idaho's governor sent a telegram to President Grover Cleveland, and Cleveland let the bill die without signing it.

shots.photo: File:Grover Cleveland, bust portrait, seated, facing right LCCN2014648289.jpg

stat.label: The bill to give the panhandle to Washington dies

paragraphs.text: The territory still had to win the north back. In January 1889 its governor signed the bill that founded the University of Idaho, and the university was put in Moscow, in the north. It helped stop the push to join Washington, and it is still there.

stat.label: University of Idaho founded in Moscow

paragraphs.text: Three years later, in 1890, Idaho became a state with the panhandle still attached. Should the north have gone to Washington? People in North Idaho still argue about it. What they did have was something the south did not: silver.

stat.label: Idaho becomes a state

shots.photo: File:Miner's Hat Realty, Kellogg, Idaho LCCN2017709172.tif

paragraphs.text: Reason four. The one place in the north that drew thousands of people also did the most damage.

In the 1880s prospectors found silver, lead and zinc along the South Fork of the Coeur d'Alene River. The narrow canyon there became the Silver Valley, with Wallace, Kellogg and Mullan strung along the river.

shots.on_screen_text: The Silver Valley from above Kellogg
The South Fork of the Coeur d'Alene

paragraphs.text: Wallace is so tight in its canyon that Interstate 90 once ran down its main street. Until 1991 it had the last traffic light on the whole interstate between Seattle and Boston. When the freeway was finally lifted over the town on a viaduct, the people of Wallace held a funeral for the light.

stat.label: The last traffic light on I-90 is removed

paragraphs.text: Since 1884 the district has produced more than a billion ounces of silver. It is one of the richest silver districts ever found on Earth.

stat.label: Silver from the Coeur d'Alene district since 1884

paragraphs.text: The money did not reach the men underground. In 1892 and again in 1899 the miners' union fought the mine owners. On the twenty-ninth of April 1899, union men seized a train, loaded it with about three thousand pounds of dynamite, and blew up the Bunker Hill company's mill at Wardner.

shots.on_screen_text: Mines and mills of the Silver Valley

stat.label: Mine wars in the Coeur d'Alene district

shots.photo: File:BUNKER HILL LEAD SMELTER. VIEW IS FROM CIA TO THE SOUTH. IN FOREGROUND, PLANT DRY, SLAG FUMING PLANT, BLAST FURNACE, SMELTER OFFICE, LEAD AND SILVER REFINERIES ARE VISIBLE, L. TO R HAER ID,40-KELL,2-2.tif
shots.on_screen_text: The Bunker Hill works at Kellogg

stat.label: Of dynamite, 29 April 1899

paragraphs.text: Governor Frank Steunenberg declared martial law. Federal troops came, and hundreds of miners were held for months in open-air pens called the bullpen.

stat.label: Shoshone County, May 1899

paragraphs.text: Six years later, on the thirtieth of December 1905, Steunenberg opened the gate of his house in Caldwell and a bomb killed him. The man who planted it, Harry Orchard, said union leaders had paid him. The union's leader Big Bill Haywood was tried for the murder in 1907, in one of the most famous trials in American labour history, and acquitted.

stat.label: Ex-governor Steunenberg killed by a bomb
Said union leaders had paid him

shots.photo: File:HAYWOOD, WILLIAM. 'BIG BILL,' LABOR AGITATOR LCCN2016866412.jpg

stat.label: Haywood's murder trial in Boise

paragraphs.text: The mines kept going. On the second of May 1972, a fire broke out deep inside the Sunshine Mine near Kellogg. One hundred and seventy-three men were underground. Smoke and carbon monoxide filled the tunnels, and ninety-one of them died. The cause was never found. It led to the federal mine safety law of 1977.

shots.on_screen_text: Big Creek, site of the Sunshine Mine

stat.label: Men underground, 2 May 1972
Died in the Sunshine Mine fire
Federal Mine Safety and Health Act

paragraphs.text: The worst damage came from above the ground. In Kellogg the Bunker Hill smelter melted lead ore. In September 1973 a fire damaged the baghouse, the great filter that caught the smoke. The company kept the smelter running without it.

shots.photo: File:BUNKER HILL LEAD SMELTER. VIEW IS FROM RIDGE ABOVE GOVERNMENT GULCH LOOKING TO THE EAST. IN THE RIGHT MID GROUND, CARPENTER SHOP BUILDINGS AND FRAMING SHEDS ARE VISIBLE. THE HAER ID,40-KELL,2-4.tif

stat.label: Baghouse fire; the smelter keeps running

shots.photo: File:PELLETIZING PLANT SECTION OF ORE PREPARATION PLANT. VIEW IS FROM WITHIN SMELTER COMPLEX LOOKING TO THE SOUTH. - Bunker Hill Lead Smelter, Bradley Rail Siding, Kellogg, Shoshone HAER ID,40-KELL,2-5.tif

paragraphs.text: Lead dust settled over the town. When the children of Kellogg were tested, their blood lead levels were some of the highest ever measured in the United States.

stat.label: Children's blood lead in Kellogg, 1974

paragraphs.text: The smelter closed in 1981. Two years later the valley became one of the country's first Superfund sites. Crews have since replaced the soil or laid clean barriers over more than seven thousand homes and businesses.

shots.photo: File:Lincoln School, Cameron Avenue, Kellogg, Idaho LCCN2017706076.tif

stat.label: The Bunker Hill site is listed
Homes and businesses given clean soil or barriers

shots.photo: File:Masonic Temple, Main Street, Kellogg, Idaho LCCN2017706247.tif

paragraphs.text: And the waste did not stay in the valley. Until 1968 most of the mines' tailings went straight into the river. About seventy-five million metric tons of sediment rich in lead and other metals now lie on the bed of Lake Coeur d'Alene, downstream.

shots.on_screen_text: Where the Coeur d'Alene River enters the lake

stat.label: Metal-rich sediment on the bed of Lake Coeur d'Alene

paragraphs.text: In 1970 Kellogg had about thirty-eight hundred people. In 2020 it had about twenty-three hundred. And the Silver Valley was not the only industry up here that collapsed.

shots.photo: File:Miner's Hat Realty, Kellogg, Idaho LCCN2017709172.tif

paragraphs.text: Kellogg has tried to turn itself around. In 1990 it opened a ski area, Silver Mountain, with a gondola that climbs three point one miles from the edge of town, the longest single-stage gondola in North America.

shots.on_screen_text: Kellogg and the slopes of Silver Mountain

stat.label: Silver Mountain gondola, opened 1990

paragraphs.text: Reason five. The forests that covered the north paid its wages for a century, and then they stopped.
Logging came with the railways. In 1906 the Potlatch Lumber Company built a whole town of its own on the edge of the Palouse, and next to it the largest white pine sawmill in the world.

shots.photo: File:The Largest Log Train on Washington, Idaho & Montana Railway, Potlatch Lumber Company, 1907 - Potlatch, Idaho (18600423811).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A log train of the Potlatch Lumber Company, 1907
The big mill at Potlatch, about 1910

paragraphs.text: Towns like Orofino, Pierce and St. Maries lived on the logs that came out of the national forests. Then, from the 1980s, there were fewer of them. Less federal land was opened for logging, machines replaced workers, and cheaper lumber came from Canada.

shots.photo: File:Log Pond and Railroad Log Dump, Potlatch Lumber Company, 1907 - Potlatch, Idaho (18572366416).jpg
File:Bird's Eye View, circa 1912 - Elk River, Idaho (4263609151).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Elk River, a mill town, about 1912

paragraphs.text: The great mill at Potlatch closed in 1983. The plywood plant near Pierce closed in 2000, and 215 people lost their jobs. In 2016 two sawmills near Orofino closed within six months of each other.

stat.label: The Potlatch mill closes
Plywood plant near Pierce closes, 2000

paragraphs.text: Where the mills closed, the young left, and the towns grew older. Should the national forests be opened to more logging to bring the jobs back? Or are they worth more standing, for water, wildlife and the people who come to see them? Idaho has argued about it for forty years.

shots.photo: File:Sawmill Looking Northeast, Potlatch Lumber Company, 1907 - Potlatch, Idaho (18411041298).jpg
File:Another Canyon View in Frank Church Wilderness.jpg
File:Along trail in Frank Church Wilderness.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A trail in the Frank Church wilderness

ask.text: Open the national forests to more logging, or keep them standing?

paragraphs.text: So we have mountains, government land, a lost capital, a poisoned valley and closed mills. And yet in one corner of the north, people are arriving faster than almost anywhere in the country.
Reason six is really the answer to the whole question. Northern Idaho is not empty. It is full in one place and empty everywhere else.

We added up the 2020 census for the ten northern counties. Kootenai County, around Coeur d'Alene, holds almost half of the north's people on six per cent of its land. Two in three northern Idahoans live within about fifteen miles of just three towns: Coeur d'Alene, Lewiston and Moscow.

stat.label: Of the north's people, on this share of its land
stat.source: Own count: 2020 census block groups, ten northern counties (geo/measure_population.py)

stat.label: Northern Idahoans within ~15 mi of three towns
stat.source: Own count: 2020 census block groups, ten northern counties (geo/measure_population.py)

paragraphs.text: Lewiston, at the southern end, even has a seaport. Barges come up the Columbia and the Snake through eight locks and dams, about four hundred and sixty-five river miles from the Pacific, and carry wheat, peas and lentils from the Palouse back down. It is the most inland seaport on the West Coast.

stat.label: Lewiston, the most inland West Coast seaport

shots.photo: File:Confluence of Clearwater and Snake rivers - Lewiston, Idaho (21116852016).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Snake and the Clearwater at Lewiston

paragraphs.text: For decades the corner around Coeur d'Alene also had a problem with its name. From the 1970s a white supremacist group, the Aryan Nations, had its compound near Hayden Lake. In 2000 a local jury ordered it to pay six point three million dollars to a mother and son its guards had fired on. The group went bankrupt, and the compound was torn down in 2001.

shots.photo: File:Honeysuckle Bay, Hayden Lake, ID - panoramio.jpg

stat.label: Jury verdict against the Aryan Nations, 2000

paragraphs.text: And Kootenai is growing. Between 2020 and 2024 it gained about seventeen thousand people, almost ten per cent. Most of the newcomers came from other states, many of them from Spokane and from Southern California.

shots.on_screen_text: Post Falls, between Spokane and Coeur d'Alene

stat.label: Kootenai County, 2020-2024

shots.photo: File:City of Coeur d'Alene, from a rooftop, 2006.jpg

paragraphs.text: It works because Coeur d'Alene is not really cut off. It sits on Interstate 90, half an hour from Spokane and its airport. The road follows the line of the Mullan Road, the first wagon road over these mountains, built between 1859 and 1862.

shots.on_screen_text: Fourth of July Pass, on the old Mullan Road

stat.label: The Mullan Road is finished

paragraphs.text: North of Coeur d'Alene lies Lake Pend Oreille, Idaho's largest lake. It is about eleven hundred and fifty feet deep, carved by the ice age.

stat.label: Depth of Lake Pend Oreille

paragraphs.text: In 1942 the US Navy built a training base on its shore, hundreds of miles from any ocean, where it was thought to be safe from Japanese bombers. In about two and a half years almost three hundred thousand sailors trained there. For a while it was the second-largest naval training station in the country.

shots.photo: File:U.S. Naval Training Staion (Lake Pend Oreille) Farragut, Idaho. - NARA - 195430.jpg

stat.label: Recruits trained at Farragut, 1942-45

shots.photo: File:U.S. Naval Training Station, (Lake Pend Oreille) Farragut, Idaho. - NARA - 195431.jpg

paragraphs.text: The base closed after the war and became Farragut State Park. But the Navy never left the lake. Its deep, quiet water is still used to test large scale models of submarines and ships.

shots.photo: File:Farragut State Park Welcome Sign, Idaho (40479710922).jpg

File:US Navy 051130-N-7676W-033 The Advanced Electric Ship Demonstrator (AESD), Sea Jet, undergoes sea trials on Lake Pend Oreille at the Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock Division, Acoustic Research Detachment in Bayview, Idah.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Navy test craft Sea Jet on Lake Pend Oreille, 2005

paragraphs.text: Now drive south from Coeur d'Alene into Idaho County, and it is a different place. Sixteen thousand people. More than eight thousand square miles, more land than New Jersey. Grangeville, its largest town, has about three thousand people.

stat.label: Idaho County: more land than New Jersey

paragraphs.text: So why does almost nobody live in northern Idaho?

Because a wall of mountains cuts it off from the rest of its state, with one road over White Bird Hill and the last highway finished in 1962. Because most of its land is federal forest, and in 1910 that forest burned on a scale nobody had seen.

shots.photo: File:White Bird Hill Grade, 1924 - White Bird, Idaho (50901386962).jpg

paragraphs.text: Because its capital was carried off to Boise by soldiers in 1865, and the bill that would have given it to Washington died on a president's desk. Because the Silver Valley gave a billion ounces of silver and left lead in its children's blood. And because the mills that replaced the mines closed one after another.

shots.photo: File:Grover Cleveland, bust portrait, seated, facing right LCCN2014648289.jpg

File:BUNKER HILL LEAD SMELTER. VIEW IS FROM CENTRAL IMPOUNDMENT AREA LOOKING SOUTH. PLANT DRY IS IN CENTER FOREGROUND, SLAG FUMING PLANT IS IN RIGHT FOREGROUND, AND BAG HOUSE IS IN HAER ID,40-KELL,2-1.tif

paragraphs.text: What is left is a north that is full in one corner around Coeur d'Alene and nearly empty everywhere else, where the clocks still run on Pacific time.
If you lived in North Idaho, would you rather be governed from Boise, or from Olympia in Washington?

ask.text: Govern North Idaho from Boise, or from Olympia in Washington?

youtube.description: Northern Idaho is a quarter of the state, bigger than Vermont and New Hampshire together, yet only about one Idahoan in five lives there, most of them around Coeur d'Alene. We follow why: the wall of mountains and the largest wilderness in the lower 48, one road over White Bird Hill, national forest that covers most of the land, the Big Burn of 1910, a territorial capital taken from Lewiston to Boise in 1865 and the 1887 bill that nearly gave the panhandle to Washington, the Silver Valley's billion ounces of silver, its mine wars, the Sunshine Mine fire and the Bunker Hill lead poisoning, the timber mills that closed, and the corner around Coeur d'Alene that is now growing fast.
